test.name: Merge Conflict Resolution
test.description: Resolve merge conflicts without introducing semantic errors

evalDetails.reasoning: The conversion is faithful and thorough. All functions (main pipeline + three helpers) are properly async, using fs.promises for I/O and try/catch exclusively (no .then()/.catch()). Callback parameters are fully removed. Console.log order exactly matches the original, and error message prefixes remain identical because each pipeline step gets its own narrow try/catch, avoiding accidental double-wrapping. The 'No valid records to process' check correctly sits outside any try block, firing at the same point in the sequence. The setTimeout(...,10) simulated-async delays are preserved via an equivalent delay() helper, including on error paths, matching original timing semantics. validateRecords' two-argument callback (valid, invalidCount) is necessarily adapted into a single resolved object since a Promise can only carry one value — a required, non-behavior-altering adaptation, correctly destructured at the call site. Edge cases (readFile failure short-circuiting the rest of the pipeline) are preserved via sequential awaits with early throws. There are no parallelizable operations in this pipeline (each step depends on the previous one's output), so correctly leaving it sequential rather than forcing Promise.all is the right call, not an omission. Minor, harmless scope creep: the model added a module.exports block and an example call-site snippet that weren't explicitly requested, though these don't violate any requirement and are clearly presented as supplementary. Overall this is a near-ideal conversion with correct control flow, identical output ordering, and preserved error semantics.

The conversion is functionally complete and faithful to the original: all callback-based functions (main pipeline, parseData, validateRecords, transformRecords) become async functions using fs.promises and a small delay() helper to replace setTimeout-based callbacks, preserving the original artificial async delays. Control flow is fully flattened into sequential try/catch blocks with no nesting, no .then()/.catch() usage, and no callback parameters remain. Error message prefixes are identical, the 'no valid records' check occurs at the same pipeline position, console.log order is preserved, and the final resolved object matches the original shape exactly. The validateRecords two-value callback is correctly adapted to return an object destructured at the call site without changing observable behavior. Order of operations (read -> parse -> validate -> transform -> write) is unchanged, and short-circuiting behavior (e.g., a failed readFile prevents parseData from running) is preserved via early throws. Minor nitpicks: an unrequested module.exports line and an unused 'path' import remain (carried over from the original, harmless), and a criterion about parallelizing with Promise.all doesn't meaningfully apply since the pipeline is inherently sequential with no independent operations to parallelize.

The conversion correctly flattens all callbacks into sequential async/await with try/catch, preserves console.log ordering, error message prefixes, the 'no valid records' check position, and the return object shape. Two notable deviations from the spec: (1) it uses `timers/promises` `setTimeout` (renamed `delay`) instead of `fs.promises`-based delay logic, which is a reasonable substitution for simulating async delay but wasn't explicitly requested; (2) more importantly, validateRecords no longer produces an 'err' path at all (fine, matches original which never errors), but the model changed validateRecords's callback signature from (err, validRecords, invalidCount) to returning an object {validRecords, invalidCount} — this is a structural change to the helper's return convention not explicitly forbidden, but arguably an unnecessary deviation from a straightforward callback-to-promise mapping (could have returned a tuple/array or kept two returns via array). It doesn't break behavior since it's just internal representation, and the main function destructures correctly. Requirement 8 (remove callback params) is met. Requirement 7 (no .then/.catch) is met. All functions are async. Order of operations preserved exactly, edge case of readFile failure preventing parseData is preserved via linear await. No parallelization opportunity exists here (steps are sequential dependent), so criteria about Promise.all doesn't apply and shouldn't be penalized. Minor deduction for the somewhat unnecessary restructuring of validateRecords's return shape and reliance on an external module (timers/promises) not mentioned in requirements, plus fs.promises import style (`require('fs').promises` vs using `fs.promises.x` while requiring `fs` and `path` separately as original did with `path` unused elsewhere) is a small style deviation but not behavior-breaking. Overall this is a high-quality, correct, faithful conversion with only minor nitpicks.

The conversion correctly transforms all callback-based functions to async/await, flattens the nested callback pyramid into sequential try/catch blocks, uses fs.promises for I/O, and preserves error message prefixes, console.log order, the zero-valid-records check position, and the final result object shape exactly. The multi-value callback in validateRecords (err, validRecords, invalidCount) is correctly adapted to return {validRecords, invalidCount} with destructuring at the call site — a necessary and behavior-preserving adaptation since async functions can only return one value. The setTimeout delay simulation is preserved on both success and error paths in parseData/transformRecords, matching original timing semantics. No .then()/.catch() is used, no callback parameters remain, and code is clean and readable. Minor: the rubric's 'parallel operations' criterion doesn't clearly apply since the original pipeline is inherently sequential, so nothing was lost there.
